name: Hassan Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Hassan, and thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy seed, fertiliser, fencing, feed and hand tools for Millbrook Agri Supply, which sells to farm shops and farmers across the valley. I start at half past seven, check what's low in the yard, and ring the mills and the merchants for prices. Planting season is the busy one, and in winter I mostly chase deliveries that the snow has held up. I'm still the junior, nine years in, because Mr Dunmore (the owner) learned the trade from his father and still does the big deals himself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you tell what a farmer will need before they ask?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is that the work is real. A farmer needs the seed on a Tuesday, and I get it there. What wears me out is the squeeze, since farmers are buying less and I'm on low pay, and the bigger firms keep undercutting us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, let's get on with it, because a hype cycle never fed anyone. To friends I'd say I'm not surprised, since people have been promising miracles since I was a boy. I'm not online much, though my son Rui sends me things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it doesn't change much for me. I've started using an AI tool now and then, which Rui showed me, to look up weather and price trends, and it's handy. Money is the problem, as I've got under a month saved and my wage is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and use the tool a little more where it saves me an hour. I'd ask Mr Dunmore to let me look after the winter fencing contracts, since I know the farmers. And I'd grow vegetables on the allotment again and sell the extra at the farm gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady. I'm not afraid of anything in that picture, but I'm never fully easy, because a bad winter or a broken boiler would put us into debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a bad year for the valley's farms mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Ana works part-time at the school canteen. Between us we pay the bills, with nothing left. If the valley's farms had a bad year, Millbrook would feel it quickly and so would I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell vegetables at the farm gate. How much might that bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what matters more than AI is the weather and the price of fertiliser. Those two things decide whether I have a job, and no machine controls either.

say: I'd say **get on**, because a hype cycle never fed anyone.
I'd tell friends people have been promising **miracles** since I was a boy.
think: It doesn't change much for me, and I already use AI for **weather and prices**.
Money is the problem, with under **a month** saved.
do: **Use** the AI tool a little more where it saves an hour.
**Ask** Mr Dunmore to let me handle the winter fencing contracts.
**Grow** vegetables on the allotment and sell the extra at the farm gate.
feel: **Steady**, but never fully easy, because a bad winter would put us in debt.
S0.quote: What matters more than AI is the weather and the price of fertiliser.
fieldNote: He is steady and already uses AI for **weather and price** checks, so the plateau holds little fear.
His real worries are money and the farm economy, which decides Millbrook's health.
The allotment is a typical practical, low-cost side move.

steps.text: Use the AI tool for weather and price trends where it saves an hour
Keep buying seed, feed and fencing for the valley farm shops
Grow vegetables on the allotment and sell extras at the farm gate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I'm willing to learn what's proven, and I'd ask Mr Dunmore to show me what he plans. To friends I'd say change is normal, but the firms who gain should help train people. At the mosque I'd say we should look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my desk is exposed. Buying, checking and planning are what the card lists, and a machine can do the paperwork faster than me. But the farmers trust me, and I think that counts for something. I'm just not sure how much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tool every day, so I'm quick and accurate, and I'd show Mr Dunmore the time it saves. I'd get my HGV licence, since a delivery driver who knows the farmers is harder to replace. And I'd put 70 a week aside from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels uncertain but not hopeless. I've seen the farm world change many times, with new tractors and new rules, and people survived by being useful. I try to hold on to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the yard would you be worried about, and what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eddie in the yard is 63 and he's worried. I'd tell him to learn the handheld scanner now, before they force it on him. I'd show him how, because it's better to learn from a friend than from a manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Rui about his work as a mechanic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also say to my son Rui, who's a mechanic at the tractor dealer, that he's in a good place. Machines still need fixing. He should keep learning the electronics, because that's where the money is going.

say: I'd tell Mr Dunmore I'm willing to learn what's **proven**.
I'd tell friends firms who gain should help **train** people.
think: My desk is **exposed**, since buying, checking and planning are what the card lists.
The farmers **trust** me, and that counts for something.
do: **Use** the AI tool daily and show Mr Dunmore the time it saves.
**Get** my HGV licence to become a delivery driver who knows the farmers.
feel: **Uncertain but not hopeless**, because the farm world has changed before.
S1.quote: A delivery driver who knows the farmers is harder to replace.
fieldNote: He plans to move from the exposed **desk** to a trusted delivery role, using relationships as protection.
Anxious: his own job could shrink, but he still feels some control.
Helps Eddie learn the scanner, showing loyalty and a sense of community.

steps.text: Use the AI tool every day and show Mr Dunmore the time it saves
Get an HGV licence to deliver to the farmers I know
Put 70 a week into savings from now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far too fast, and somebody should be accountable. At the mosque I'd ask us to gather and help families who lose work. At work I'd tell Mr Dunmore to be honest about what the firm can survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is gone. The paperwork can all be done by a machine in a fraction of the time, and I'm paid little, so I'd go first. Two years gives me no time to build a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the plain things. I'd cut every extra and save everything I could, and I'd talk to Ana that same night. I'd ask the mosque committee about the hardship fund, and I'd go to the council to see what help there is, though I don't like asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a field flooding in the spring. There's nothing to do but watch it and plan where to put the sandbags. I'd be quietly scared, and I'd hide it from Ana, though she'd see through me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to your wife Ana that same night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Sofia is a dental receptionist, and her job is partly screens, so she's exposed too. I'd say we all keep our spending low and stay together. We've always done it that way in my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd not take on debt. What happened to your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd not do is run up debt to carry on as before. If I take out a loan with nothing to pay it back, that's worse than doing without. I've seen that happen to my brother, and I won't do it.

say: I'd say it's **far too fast** and somebody should be accountable.
I'd tell Mr Dunmore to be **honest** about what the firm can survive.
think: My job is **gone**, because a machine can do the paperwork faster and I'm paid little.
Two years gives me **no time** to build a cushion.
do: **Cut** every extra and save everything I can.
**Ask** the mosque committee about the hardship fund.
**Go** to the council to see what help there is.
feel: Like a **field flooding**, quietly scared and hiding it from Ana.
S2.quote: If I take out a loan with nothing to pay it back, that's worse than doing without.
fieldNote: He expects his job to go and plans conservatively, refusing **debt**.
Community help, mosque and council, comes second and reluctantly.
Family cohesion is how he frames resilience.

steps.text: Cut every extra and keep spending to food, rent and heating
Put every spare pound into savings from the first week
Ask the mosque committee and the council about hardship help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning if people take it seriously. At work I'd say Millbrook should plan its training now. To friends I'd say the firms that gain from this should help pay for it, and I'd vote for people who say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I could get through it. I'd be 63, and if I move to delivery or yard supervision, I'd have the robot delay on my side. The part I fear is the money. I'd need savings and I've got hardly any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the HGV licence in the first year and look for a driving or yard job at Millbrook. I'd use the AI tool until I'm good at it, so I'm useful in both worlds. And I'd save 100 a week, even if I need to take on extra weekend shifts at the farm shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long winter ahead with enough firewood if I work hard. I think I'd sleep fine most nights, though not all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you couldn't do in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots coming three years after the thinking AI helps the hands-on jobs like driving and yard work. A delivery driver who knows every farm gate is not easy to replace, and I'd like to be that driver in 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and your wife Ana feel about taking in a lodger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ana we may need to rent out the box room to a lodger for a few years. She'd say yes, because we've done it before when the children were small. A bit of extra rent would help us build a cushion.

say: I'd say five years is a **decent warning** if people take it seriously.
I'd vote for people who say **firms that gain** should help pay for training.
think: I could get through it if I move to **delivery or yard** work.
My fear is the **money**, because I've got hardly any savings.
do: **Get** the HGV licence in the first year.
**Learn** the AI tool until I'm useful in both worlds.
**Save** 100 a week and take weekend shifts at the farm shop.
feel: Like a **long winter** ahead, with enough firewood if I work hard.
S3.quote: A delivery driver who knows every farm gate is not easy to replace, and I'd like to be that driver in 2032.
fieldNote: Five years makes his plan realistic: **HGV** licence, delivery role, and the robot delay on his side.
Anxious because the money to fund the plan isn't there yet.
The lodger idea shows practical thinking, using the household's assets.

steps.text: Get an HGV licence in the first year
Ask Mr Dunmore for a driving or yard job at Millbrook
Save 100 a week with weekend shifts at the farm shop
Use the AI tool until I'm useful on screen and in the yard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it right, if the people in charge bother. At work I'd keep up with the job. At the mosque I'd say let's teach the young a trade and some self-reliance, since that has always been the best insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 68 by then, so I think I'd be retired. My worry is that the pension won't stretch. If I save steadily, I'd have a modest cushion, but nothing extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 65, learn the tools I need and save 60 a week for the next seven years. I'd offer to train the young staff at Millbrook, because teaching is a good use of experience. And I'd help Rui and Sofia think about their futures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels distant, and I'd call it manageable. I'd still think about it, but I wouldn't lose sleep. I'd feel sorry for the young ones who have to live with it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Sofia about her reception job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sofia to move out of reception work within a few years, maybe into dental nursing, which is hands-on. I'd tell Rui to stay in the workshop. Machines can do thinking work first, so I'd keep both on the hands-on side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a normal retirement look like for you and Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What changes with ten years is that I can work to a normal retirement and go out on my feet. With two years I'd be out and scared. Here I'd go home at 65 with my head up.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough** to do it right if the people in charge bother.
I'd tell the mosque to teach the young a **trade** and self-reliance.
think: I'd be 68 by then, so I think I'd be **retired**.
My worry is that the **pension** won't stretch.
do: **Work** to 65 and save 60 a week for seven years.
**Offer** to train the young staff at Millbrook.
**Help** Rui and Sofia think about their futures.
feel: **Distant** and manageable, with some sorrow for the young ones.
S4.quote: I'd go home at 65 with my head up.
fieldNote: Ten years takes AGI past his working life; his mood is **uneasy**, not calm, because of the pension.
Wants to teach and mentor, a natural fit with his traditional values.
Advice to his children rests on the thinking-first, hands-on-later order.

steps.text: Save 60 a week for the next seven years
Keep working at Millbrook until 65 and train the young staff
Talk with Sofia about dental nursing, a hands-on job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2031 one worries me most. It's near enough that I'd be working through it, at 63, but not so near that I could say it's a long shot. I'd have a bit of time, but not enough money to use it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't asking for charity. We'd like a fair chance to keep working, with proper training, and some help while we're learning. That's not too much to ask.

headlineQuote: We'd like a fair chance to keep working, with proper training, and some help while we're learning.
portrait: Hassan is 58, a junior buyer at **Millbrook Agri Supply**, a farm supplier, with a wife and two grown children.
He is **steady**: he uses AI now and then, and learns new tools when he sees they're proven.
He is **traditional**, values work and apprenticeships over handouts, and leans on his mosque and family.
His plan in the faster pictures is to move to **delivery or yard** work, using farmers' trust and the robot delay.
His real constraint is **money**, with under a month saved, which keeps him anxious even when time allows.
biggestWorry: The **2031** picture, near enough to hit him at 63 but with too little money to use the time.
whatWouldHelp: A fair chance with **proper training**, some help while he learns, and a pension that stretches.
